Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and alert you when hypertension may be present, but they won't give you an actual blood pressure reading.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can do this, but they require periodic calibration with a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to offer full blood pressure measurement capabilities without any calibration, citing clinical trial results involving thousands of participants...

The Silent Killer

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) both pose serious health threats.

Of the two, hypertension is more dangerous and is even called the "silent killer" — it can cause serious and irreversible damage to your arteries, heart and brain, yet shows no obvious symptoms. Many people only discover they have the condition after suffering a heart attack or stroke.

For elderly individuals, regular blood pressure monitoring is ideal. While there are many easy-to-use home upper-arm blood pressure monitors on the market, a fitness device that can be worn all day and monitor automatically would be even more ideal.

Apple Watch Blood Pressure Feature

With the launch of watchOS 26, five Apple Watch models can now measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models won't provide any readings — they only alert you when they detect possible signs of hypertension. Other devices like the Oura Ring work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices on the market can provide actual blood pressure readings, but they require periodic calibration using readings from an upper-arm blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals says its Signal Ring smart ring requires no calibration, yet can deliver accuracy comparable to traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitors.

CEO Tom Moss told Bloomberg that he himself nearly died from undiagnosed hypertension — an experience that motivated him to found the company.

The Signal Ring will begin taking orders later today, ship in October, and is priced at US$399 with no subscription fees required. The accompanying mobile app can display real-time blood pressure readings and long-term trends (as shown in the image above).

Worth noting is that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), although clinical trials have shown it can deliver accurate blood pressure readings for thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss himself isn't particularly keen on marketing the Signal Ring to all consumers. He says the feature is best suited for elderly individuals and those assessed by doctors as being at risk of hypertension — comments that hint the Signal Ring may not excel in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
